question: Why train the model on (r₁, r₂, cos θ) instead of the 9 Cartesian coordinates?

answers.answer: The energy can't change when the molecule is translated or rotated; these features already have that symmetry, so the model doesn't have to learn it
answers.feedback: Right: build the physics into the inputs.

answers.answer: Three numbers are faster to type
answers.feedback: Speed is a bonus; the reason is symmetry.

answers.answer: Cartesian coordinates can't describe a bent molecule
answers.feedback: They describe any geometry, but they change when the molecule moves, while the energy doesn't.

answers.answer: DFT needs internal coordinates
answers.feedback: PySCF takes Cartesian coordinates.

question: Why is every training point entered twice, with r₁ and r₂ swapped?

answers.answer: The two O atoms are identical, so E(r₁, r₂, cos θ) = E(r₂, r₁, cos θ); the swapped copies enforce that permutation symmetry
answers.feedback: Right.

answers.answer: To double the size of the test set
answers.feedback: The test set is separate and is never used for training.

answers.answer: To reduce the DFT noise
answers.feedback: The copies have the same energy; they add symmetry, not new information about noise.

answers.answer: It makes the GP train faster
answers.feedback: It doubles the training set, so training is slower.

question: Why must the model be judged on a held-out test set rather than on its training data?

answers.answer: A flexible model can fit its training points almost exactly while being wrong in between; only unseen data tests whether it has learned the surface
answers.feedback: Right: the training error measures memory, the test error measures learning.

answers.answer: The training data are less accurate
answers.feedback: Both are B3LYP/def2-SVP.

answers.answer: The test set is larger
answers.feedback: It is smaller (100 vs 320).

answers.answer: Gaussian processes cannot predict training points
answers.feedback: They can, very accurately; that is exactly why the training error is misleading.

question: The learning curve levels off near 0.02 meV. What sets this floor?

answers.answer: The numerical noise of the DFT reference energies (the integration grid), which no amount of data removes
answers.feedback: Right.

answers.answer: The speed of the computer
answers.feedback: Accuracy doesn't depend on speed.

answers.answer: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation
answers.feedback: Both the data and the model live on the same Born–Oppenheimer surface.

answers.answer: The model has stopped learning because it is full
answers.feedback: A GP keeps improving as long as the data contain information; the floor is in the data.

question: Along a bond stretch beyond the training range, the GP energy goes wrong. How can you tell from the GP alone?

answers.answer: Its predicted uncertainty σ grows rapidly outside the region covered by training data
answers.feedback: Right: a GP knows when it is extrapolating.

answers.answer: The energy becomes negative
answers.feedback: It may or may not; the uncertainty is the reliable warning.

answers.answer: You can't; you always need a DFT check
answers.feedback: A DFT check confirms it, but the GP's σ already warns you.

answers.answer: The features become complex numbers
answers.feedback: The features stay real for any geometry.
